rationale:
Evidence: iteration 8 (kp 2.0, kd 1.5, base_speed 0.9, sensors at y=0.08, 16 mm footprint, mass 0.6 kg) is the best design so far at 473.6. Its oval finished 18 of 20, the s-bend finished 6 of 20 (progress 0.74), and the slalom always ends off track at progress about 0.15 with max_error about 0.063 m. Two comparisons isolate the levers. Raising kp to 2.4 (iteration 7) overshot on the s-bend and dropped the score to 431. Lowering base_speed to 0.85 (iteration 9) lost s-bend finishes (6 to 2 of 20) and scored 429, so speed 0.9 is the better point and I keep it. Raising kd from 1.0 to 1.5 (iteration 6 to 8) helped the s-bend, from 4 to 6 finishes, with oscillation falling from 0.38 to 0.37. The derivative term is therefore the most productive lever that has not reached a limit yet. Sensors are at the forward limit (y=0.08), and the off-track limit stays at the 0.06 m floor for every allowed body width, so geometry cannot widen it.

Change: kd raised from 1.5 to 2.0. Everything else is held at iteration 8: kp 2.0, ki 0, base_speed 0.9, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], last_direction line loss, and the same geometry. This is a single-factor test. Derivative damping should reduce the overshoot that limits the s-bend and slalom. At a full edge signal of 2, the signal change per step stays bounded, and turn stays within the wheel-command limits at base PWM 1843.

Expected result: oval completion stays around 90 percent or better. The s-bend finish rate rises from 30 percent toward 40 to 50 percent, and s-bend progress moves above 0.75. Score target is about 490 to 540. Main risk: kd 2.0 amplifies sensor noise and jitter, which would lower the oval finish rate. The revision rounds should check this against the critique.
